headline: Agentic Software Development shifts AI from assistants to goal-driven agents for full tasks
summary: AI is evolving beyond prompt-response assistance. Agentic AI aims to complete entire software tasks autonomously, planning, executing, and refining until the objective is met.
details: AI has become a regular part of many development workflows, used for debugging, boilerplate code, or explaining concepts. Traditionally, developers treat AI as an assistant responding to prompts.

Agentic Software Development introduces a new paradigm where AI is given a goal instead of single tasks. This allows the AI to plan, break down work, generate code, run tests, and fix problems autonomously.

The core idea is an "execution loop" where the agent evaluates its own progress and decides the next action until the objective is achieved. This moves beyond the traditional ask-and-wait interaction.

While AI may automate implementation, developers remain crucial for understanding requirements, designing architecture, and ensuring security, accessibility, and performance. The human role shifts to higher-level decision-making.

Frontend developers can envision AI agents handling repetitive work like setting up project structures, creating reusable components, connecting APIs, writing tests, and updating documentation. This frees up time for product thinking and user experience.
The shift is from AI writing better code to AI helping complete entire software tasks. This progression means moving from asking AI for answers to giving it objectives.

headline_marked: [[Developer audits 15 Android apps for accessibility]]; AI agent becomes audit tool
headline: Developer audits 15 Android apps for accessibility; AI agent becomes audit tool
summary: A developer spent a week auditing Android apps for accessibility, finding major tech apps automatable while local banking and government apps were completely inaccessible to automated tools. This experience is transforming their AI agent into a dedicated audit
details: A developer dedicated a week to meticulously audit 15 Android applications for accessibility. This intensive review aimed to understand the current state of app accessibility and the potential for automated testing. The findings revealed significant disparities across different app categories.

Major applications like WhatsApp and those from Google demonstrated high levels of automatable accessibility. Their interfaces and underlying code were structured in a way that allowed an AI agent to effectively interact with and assess their accessibility features. This suggests a strong adherence to accessibility standards in large tech companies.

In stark contrast, local banking and government applications proved to be "completely invisible" to automated accessibility tools. This indicates a severe lack of proper implementation for accessibility, making them difficult or impossible for assistive technologies to navigate. Such findings highlight a critical gap in digital inclusion.

The insights gained from this audit are now directly influencing the developer's ongoing project. Their AI agent, initially designed for other purposes, is being refined and developed into a specialized accessibility audit tool, leveraging the lessons learned from both automatable and inaccessible apps.
